Sir GEORGE FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 58, to amend the Canada Grain Act.
He said: The purpose of this Bill is to amend section 207 of the Canada Grain Act by addling to it a clause which shall be named clause "e." I will read the section so that it may he on Hansard. It- is in reference to the powers of the Board of Grain Commissioners:
The board may in its discretion order cars to be supplied contrary to the provisions of this part (a) to elevators that are in danger of collapse ; (to) to places where grain is damp and thereby liable to become damper; (c) for the purpose of distributing seed grain to any point in the western division ; (d) in case where the operator of any country elevator reports in writing under oath that some portion of the grain in such elevator is heated and that in order to preserve such grain it is necessary to ship such heated grain to a terminal elevator for treatment, provided, however, that no relief shall be granted in such last-mentioned case as long as the warehouseman has sufficient room in his building for the rehandling of such grain.
Section " e," which it is proposed to add by way of amendment, reads as follows:
(e) whenever, after due examination, the board considers it necessary and advisable in order to relieve congestion and facilitate the despatch of grain.
It is proposed to give that additional discretionary power to the Board of Grain Commissioners. That amendment was proposed when the Act was last under discussion in the House; it was, I think, passed by the House, but was not passed by the Senate, and so did not become law. Wi'h the peculiar condition of things in the W«3t

at the present time, particularly with reference to congested districts, not only where there is a congestion of grain but where a large portion of that grain is unhoused and therefore exposed to danger and deterioration and loss as soon as the warm weather sets in, it is proposed, under this added power given to the Board of Grain Commissioners, to enable them, despite the other sections of the Act, to order in special cars for -the relief of that kind of distress. I will not go into an argument with reference to it. I think that hon. gentlemen, particularly from the Northwest, who know the present condition of things, will feel that it is necessary that this added power be given in order to provide for relief in these instances. I would ask hon. members to look into the Bill and, when we come to it the second time, put it'through', if possible.
Motion agreed to, and Bill- read the first time.

On motion of Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries), the House went into committee on the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Vancouver Harbour Commissioners Act, chapter 54, of the statutes of 1913, by providing that the corporation may make by-laws for the imposition of tolls, rates, fees and dues, other than pilotage dues, sick mariners' dues and steamboat inspection fees.

Before my hon. friend
the Minister of Marine and Fisheries asks the committee to go into the consideration of this resolution, I would like to call his attention to the fact that last evening at the close of business, when the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) was leading the House, he was asked what would be the business taken to-morrow, and the reply was:	" We will go into Supply,
taking up the Estimates of the Department of Labour, Marine and Fisheries," etc. If I had known this resolution was coming up to-day I would have asked my hon. friend to be prepared to give the committee a full statement with regard to the work the Vancouver Harbour Commissioners are

carrying on. I understand that there is a good deal of dissatisfaction in the minds of the people of Vancouver in regard to this work, and I think it is desirable that the reclamation and other work which the commissioners are doing should be fully explained to the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We could let the resolution pass, -and I would be prepared to give a full statement on the first reading of the Bill.

All right, on that understanding.	/
Mr. HAZfiN: I do not wish to enter into a discussion just now, hut my information with regard to the work the commissioners are doing in Vancouver is diametrically opposed to that of my hon. friend.

There have been some
differences of opinion among the people of Vancouver recently, as instanced by the election there a few days -ago, and perhaps my hon. friend is not correctly informed as to public sentiment with regard to the work of the Harbour Commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think my hon.
friend wishes to question the competency of the Vancouver Harbour Commission. If this resolution p,asses, the Bill founded thereon will provide an amendment to the present Act by striking out a few words. The Vancouver Harbour Commission was created by Act of tins Parliament in 19x3, and among other powers conferred upon the commissioners was the power to make bylaws for various purposes. Subsection " t " of section 19 of the Act deals with the power of the commissioners to impose tolls, and is as follows:
(t) The imposition of such tolls, rates, fees and dues, other than pilotage dues, sick mariners' fees, and steamboat inspection fees, as would be payable in the case of a harbour to which the Canada Shipping Act applies.
The amendment strikes out this subsection, and substitutes another, which is exactly the same in every respect, except that the words " as would be payable in the case of a harbour to which the Canada Shipping Act applies " are stricken out. The reason is that the words which it is proposed to strike out preclude the commissioners from making any charges for harbour dues, other than those provided in the Canada Shipping Act; or, in other words, tonnage dues in Vancouver harbour should not exceed the rates prescribed by

the Canada Shipping Act, or a maximum of $5 per entry for two entries, hut not payable more than twice in any calendar year.
It is necessary that further revenues should be obtained if the Victoria Harbour Commissioners are to carry on their work efficiently, and the amendment will enable the commissioners to raise more revenue. Of course, whatever by-laws the commissioners pqss are subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. My information is that this matter has been taken up with the shipping companies whose ships use Vancouver harbour, and who are interested in its development and proper maintenance, and that the amendment meets with their approval. They are anxious that the commissioners should have funds to maintain the harbour properly, and are willing to pay their proper contribution, in order that proper appliances may be obtained for fighting fire along the wharves and docks at the water-front, and that the harbour may be well managed and up-to-date. I shall be very glad to give my hon. friend the information which he desires on the first reading of the Bill.

I shall be glad if my hon. friend will give the committee that information on the first reading of the Bill, and also, some information with regard to the work at False creek. I am told that instead of enlarging the facilities for shipping there, the commission are really engaged in filling in False creek, for the benefit, I suppose, of some of the railway companies. Another point on which I should like some information, because it' is allied with harbour development work, is the contract which has been1 given to the Amalgamated Dry Dock Construction Company, for the erection of a dry dock, I am told. I am informed that the company has been allowed to take in the real estate for the building of that dry dock, for what seems to be the enormous sum of something over $500,000, and that they will receive interest from the Government upon that sum in the way of subsidy.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That does not come under my department, but under Public Works.

It is a Government matter and closely connected with the harbour development. I am told that upon these two matters there is very, very strong feeling among the people of, Vancouver,
and I have been asked to get all the in- 1 formation I possibly could upon the subject.

I do not wish to delay the committee at any length, but I am quite certain that my hon. friend from St. John is misinformed on this subject. The work he refers to at False creek is the reclamation of a tidal flat which is bare at every tide. Consequently, the work the commissioners are doing there could not possibly increase the obstructions to navigation. Furthermore, the channel, which was only two feet deep at low tide, is being dredged. to 22 feet, and it will be 350 feet wide. This tidal flat is being reclaimed by the Harbour Commission, and is not being leased or given away to railway companies. The Harbour Commission are going to lease it for industrial purposes, and the grant from the Government to the Harbour Commission includes a clause preventing them from subletting the land without the approval of the Governor in Cbuncil. So that my hon. friend will recognize the item when the matter comes up again, I would point out that this is the very piece of property in reference to which he had an Order in Council prepared when he was Minister of Public Works, giving the land to private individuals to exploit. At that time I was a member of the city council of Vancouver, and bitterly opposed that proposition. We succeeded in sending down a resolution from the city council, and eventually the Order in Council was not passed.
What was the date of that?

About 1910. I can give my hon. friend the exact date later. The policy of the city council then-and it always has been the policy of the city of Vancouver as a whole-was to have such lands controlled by public bodies, for public purposes, and not alienated by private interests. A few of those whose interests are affected certainly oppose this policy of public control. With the dry dock the harbour commissioners have nothing to do at all. The dry dock is very badly needed, and would have been under construction but for the outbreak of the war. It was granted under the Dry Dock Subsidy Act, and not one dollar will be included in the Estimates which is not carefully checked over by the chief engineer of the department. I do not think that should be considered in connection with the activities of

the Harbour Board. When the matter, if it is to be delayed, comes up again, I shall be most happy to give all the information I have, and the minister also will have much more information to give.
I shall be very thankful for full'information. My hon. friend refers to an Order in Council which was being prepared in 1910 for handing over False creek to private parties.
The portion to which my hon. friend refers is now being reclaimed by the Harbour Board. It comprises forty-two acres.
My recollection does not agree with that of my hon. friend. I remember that some question came up on an application from the city of Vancouver to be given control.
That is another portion altogether.

I do not remember any application to give any part of the harbour to the control of private individuals. My hon. friend may be right, because one cannot remember all that took place, but I would be very glad if he would produce a copy of the report in regard to the matter.
Certainly. There is a copy on file.	r

There must be a report either from myself or from the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and, as my hon. friend has the matter in hand, probably he will be able to produce a copy when the time comes.
Yes.
With regard to the dry-dock, which, my hon, Mend says has nothing to do with the harbour, I beg to differ from him.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Nothing to do with the Harbour Commissioners.

Still it has to do with the whole question of harbour improvement; and, if the Government is a party to the payment of the enormous sum of half a million dollars for land in connection with the drydock ^way over on the northern side of Burrard inlet-and such an amount is very excessive, because, if

the Government pays 34 or 4 per cent on that for 35 years, it is almost equivalent to the Government paying for the land- the Government will not be so ready to give grants of other moneys for the necessary development of the harbour of Vancouver. Therefore, in the interest of my hon. friend, who, I am told, has had a great deal to do in pressing forward the matter of this drydock, it would be desirable to give to the House and to the public generally all information w>th regard to these matters.

Yesterday my hon. friend from West Kent (Mr. McCoig) asked a question in reference to Government inspection of hogs, and I told him that I would get the information and give it to him to-day. I find m.y !hon. friend's words reported in Hansard as follows:
Mr. McCoig:	Mr. Speaker, I would like to
draw the attention of the Government to the market quotations in the London Free Press. The quotation for hogs is as follows:
Hogs, fed and watered, $9.50, less one-half of one per cent for Government inspection.
I would like to call the attention of the Government to the fact that hog buyers throughout the country have been deducting the price of hogs one-half of one per cent for the government inspectors. As I understand, the inspectors who are employed by the Government are paid by the Government. If these men have been collecting this percentage, have they been returning it to the Government, or have they any right to make this claim upon the farmers who are selling hogs to them?
I called the attention of the Veterinary General of the Department of Agriculture to the matter, and have received from him this memorandum:
I have been informed that the custom has arisen during the last year or two of deducting from the price paid to drovers or farmers one-half of one per cent on all hogs purchased. This deduction has apparently been agreed upon by the Canadian packers as in their opinion a fair equivalent for the losses which they suffer through animals condemned by Government inspection and pronounced unfit for food.

The money which is thus deducted from the purchase price of the hogs is retained by the purchaser and in no way goes to cover the cost of Government inspectors, their salaries being paid by the Dominion Government. It is misleading to state that one-half of one per cent is deducted for Government inspection; such is not the case. It is deducted for the benefit of the packer and to compensate him for possible losses from condemnations.

speechtext:
Having received a telegram from Halifax on the subject, I desire to call the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to the fact that the situation there in reference to coal used for bunkering, manufacturing, and domestic purposes is quite serious, owing to the lack of shipping. A great
fMr. Roche. 1
number of steamers owned and operated by the Dominion Coal Company hjive been commandeered by the Admiralty. Only yesterday, another boat owned by them, the Maslkinonge, was commandeered. The effect will toe rather disastrous, as it seems that in many parts of Nova Scotia a greater coal supply is absolutely necessary. In Halifax it is particularly important to get bunkering coal for transatlantic and West India boats. I will hand the exact information to the minister, but generally I would impress upon him the necessity of activity in this matter. I am hardly in a position to criticise the action of the Admiralty, but I have heard it stated toy shipping men in Canada that there was a lack of method and organization in the manner in which some shipping was commandeered, and I understand that their action in Great Britain has been subject to severe comment there. However, I am not arguing that point; but I wish to urge upon the minister the fact that quite a serious situation confronts us, and that we should have from his department the greatest activity possible in order to meet that situation.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: COAL SHORTAGE IN NOVA SCOTIA- LACK OF SHIPS.

For some time past this matter has been receiving the consideration and attention of my department, and of the Prime Minister also. The vessels belonging to the Dominion Coal Company which have been commandeered have been taken by the British Government for military purposes. The facts of the case, including a statement of the difficulties that may result, have been placed before the British Government through the actirig High Commissioner, Sir George Perley, and are being fully considered by the Admiralty and by the War Office. It is stated by the Admiralty that they regret having to take this course of commandeering vessels in the merchant trade, but are doing so simply because of military necessity made all the greater by reason of the fact that they have to transport not only their own troops but the troops of other countries. I shall be glad to show my hon. friend the correspondence we have h,ad on the subject. There are matters in connection with it that, perhaps, it would not be desirable to make public, but I shall have no hesitation in showing the documents to my hon. friend.
I can only say that the matter has been placed before the Imperial authorities, and I think arrangements are being made by

which, I trust, the inconvenience which the people of Halifax and St. John, even more, I think, than the people of my hoa. friend's constituency, have suffered, will be remedied.

The object of the exceptions will be obvious. Companies must maintain actua-

rial reserves in respect to tlieir policies in force outside of Canada and they are also obliged under the terms of the policy to make loans upon their policies. We are dealing only with the matter of net ledger assets in the case of Canadian companies. In regard to non-Canadian companies, it is provided:
After the fifteenth day of February, one thousand nine hundred and sixteen-
Which was the date of the Budget speech.
-and deposit of securities in respect of the business of life insurance required or permitted by the Insurance Act, 1910, to be made prior to the first day of January, one thousand nine hundred and eighteen, with the Receiver General or with a Canadian trustee or trustees appointed under and for the purposes of the said Act by any company licensed under the said Act to transact the business of life insurance in Canada other than a Canadian company shall consist of securities of Canada.
The securities of Canada are defined in the interpretation clause of the Act as being "debentures, debenture stock, bonds or other securities of Canada payable only in the currency of Canada." We have less hesitation in introducing the measure because life insurance companies, for reasons which I shall go into when the taxation measure is under consideration, have been exempted from its provisions. In addition, under the present conditions, the securities of the Dominion yield a fairly high rate of interest. Of course, they can obtain no better class of investment either for themselves or for their policyholders.
Mr. SINCLAIR! Does it relate to future investments only?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It relates to the years 1916 and 1917. Every Canadian insurance company must, during the present year, invest, if it has not yet already invested, in the securities of Canada, to an amount of not less than fifty per cent of the increase in the net ledger assets of the company during the year 1915.
Will that involve the sale of some of their present investments?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think not. The life insurance companies, as far as I know, raise no objection to the proposed legislation. I think it advisable, unless the House thinks otherwise, to refer this Bill to the Banking and Commerce Committee, so that it will receive full consideration, and so that, if any persons desire to be heard, the committee may hear them.

It seems unfair to municipalities and provinces whose bonds are so

largely held by insurance companies that it should be limited entirely to the securities of the Dominion of Canada. I do not see why it is considered desirable to discriminate as between Canada and the various provinces, cities and municipalities in Canada. It would seem to me that if a life insurance company, instead of investing in foreign securities, as many of them have done in the past, should place their investments in Dominion, provincial, or Canadian municipal bonds, that ought to be sufficient. The various municipalities, as are also the provinces, are interested in getting a fair rate for their bonds. They are all carrying on works of importance to the country at large and they are making contributions for the purposes of war. I think I am safe in saying that all of the provinces, cities and municipalities have made contributions for the purpose of assisting the Empire in connection with the war. They have contributed for patriotic purposes to the Red Cross Fund, the Patriotic Fund and other funds. I do not see why, in legislation providing for investments in purely Canadian securities, it should be declared as a condition to these companies doing business in Canada, that they must take fifty per cent at least of the securities of the Dominion of Canada. Unless the minister has information to the contrary, I would suppose that it might necessitate these companies getting rid of provincial and municipal securities. Then, take section 5 in regard to securities which companies may be required to deposit under the Insurance Act of 1910 prior to the first of January, 1918; these securities must be entirely the securities of Canada expressly excluding the bonds of the various provinces or municipalities which might yield a little higher rate of interest, but which [DOT]Would be just as safe a security for the insurance company as the bonds of the Dominion of Canada. There ought to be some pretty strong reasons presented for excluding under this Bill the securities of the various provinces and municipalities.

I suppose one
answer that would be urged against the objection made by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) is, that it is very much easier for the municipalities to market their bonds in the United States than for the Dominion of Canada to sell war issues in the United States or in any other market. When the minister referred to this matter in his Budget speech, I was inclined to inquire whether it might not be wise to take

steps to mobilize foreign securities held in this country, or at least to take power to ascertain the volume of foreign securities held here. I remember seeing some years ago, a statement issued by one of our Canadian banks giving a list of its securities, and I was impressed with the large volume of foreign issues which they held as investments. Doubtless the 'Government of Canada will have to make further war loans, and it struck me that some arrangement could be made whereby our railways, and banks, and other large corporations could make a disposition of their foreign securities and re-invest in Canadian war loans. 'Perhaps the minister has given consideration to that point; possibly, there may be very little in it. As the minister knows, the British Government have taken steps to mobilize all foreign securities held in England, and they are disposing of them from time to time in order to stabilize exchange. I think this might be worth looking into in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
With reference
to tire observations of my hon. friend from St. John, I should be disposed to concur in his views if times were normal, but if we were not at war, this legislation would not be brought down. It is purely a war measure, and arises out of the necessities of the situation with which we are confronted. I have already explained to the House that our expenditure for the war this year may reach $250,000,000, and we are confronted with a financial situation which will involve finding four hundred and twenty-five million dollars or more. Of course, to meet that expenditure, we shall have our revenues to the extent that they are available; but after we have taken that into consideration we are still confronted with a very serious financial situation by reason of the war, and next year we shall be confronted with an equally serious situation. I do not mean to say for one moment that we shall not be able to meet that situation. I am quite sure that we shall b'e able to meet it, but at the same time it is not to be disguised that the raising of these large sums of money is not, and will not be, an easy achievement. It is, therefore, necessary for us to avail ourselves of any method of adding to our market. This legislation imposes no hardship upon life insurance companies, for the reasons that I have given, and I do not think that it should be objected to by municipalities, or provinces, for the reason that the Dominion has to bear the heaviest burden of the war. It is true, as my hon. friend has said, that the
municipalities and provinces have done admirably in contributing to patriotic and other funds, and that they are manfully bearing their part in the war. But when all that has been said, the fact remains that the chief stress and strain of the war falls upon the Dominion exchequer. I do not think it is necessary for me to cite analogous legislation, but the instance which occurs to one's mind most readily is that of the United States during the Civil War. Hon. gentlemen no doubt know that the American banking system dates back to the expedients adopted during the Civil War, when Congress, in order to provide a market for the securities of the United States, legislated that note circulation should be secured by United States bonds.
There is quite a difference between the American legislation and this proposal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The American
legislation made an- artificial market for American securities; it compelled the banks to take securities as cover for their note circulation. I think it would be competent for the Dominion Government, even in ordinary times, to provide that life insurance companies should hold a certain portion of Dominion, provincial or municipal securities; I do not think that would be unsound legislation at any time. But this legislation is frankly a war measure, limited to this year and next. It will be of material assistance to the Government in raising money for war purposes.
Have the life insurance companies been consulted with regard to this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not specially, but so far as I can learn they do not object to it. I think they regard it as reasonable.

Which section of this
Bill will cover foreign insurance companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Section 5.

Why is that section
limited? Why should it not be applied to all foreign companies licensed to do business in Canada? Why should they not be compelled to make certain deposits consisting of Dominion bonds, etc.? We know that foreign insurance companies are doing an enormous " life " business in Canada. Why should they not be required, as a condition of obtaining a license to hold a certain amount of Canadian securities? Take one of the big New York companies, like the

Equitable, a company which I suppose has $500,000,000 of securities, and is doing a very large business in Canada. I am only mentioning the Equitable as one of the big American companies. I think it might very well be provided that these foreign companies should, as a condition of their receiving' a license to do business in Canada, invest in Canadian securities to an extent proportionate to the business they are doing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Bill goes further than my hon. friend suggests. My hon. friend is probably aware that, as the business of foreign life insurance companies in Canada increases they must increase their deposits, which are held, either by the Receiver General or by trustees, as security for their policyholders in this country. Now, this Bill has in contemplation that such deposits shall, until the first day of January, 1918, be made in Canadian securities only; that is to say, such companies shall not be permitted to deposit any other securities.
That is only for the increases.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. It would be rather harsh legislation to compel them to sell the vast amount of securities that are now held by the Receiver General or by trustees for the security of policyholders here, and to invest in Dominion securities, which would take the place of the securities. Under the measure as drafted, we provide that Canadian insurance companies shall deposit a certain increase of their net ledger assets in Canadian securities. Now, in order to be fair to them and also to provide an additional market for Canadian securities, we propose to enact that nonCanadian companies, which are required to make deposits in respect of their increased business in Canada, shall make such deposits in Canadian securities. So that the Bill would, seem to put both Canadian and non-Canadian companies on all-fours. It must be remembered that they are in competition one with another, and it would not be fair to deal with one class of companies without at the same time dealing with the other.

I am not able to see that. This section only requires the foreign companies tp make those additional deposits that are rendered necessary by the increased business between now and the first of January, 1918, in Canadian securities. But we know that foreign life insurance companies, such as the Equitable Life of New York,

which 1 have already mentioned, the New York Life, the Mutual Life of New York, and the English companies, do an enormous amount of life insurance business in Canada, and they are required to make deposits of securities to be approved by the Minister of Finance. Where would be the hardship in requiring those companies to convert their foreign securities into securities of Canada as a condition of their .being permitted to continue doing business? If their foreign securities are good, they can easily be converted into cash in the United States. There is a plethora of money in the United States seeking reasonably good security, and it would be the easiest thing in the world for those companies to get rid of their American securities, and there would be no hardship whatever in requiring them to substitute securities of Canada for such securities. I have always thought that in normal times foreign companies should be compelled to invest in securities of Canada, of the provinces, or of the various municipalities. In' these war times, when, as the minister says, there is difficulty in raising money and when we are imposing these exceptional taxes upon the people, there can be no ground of complaint if we require these foreign companies to convert into securities of Canada their foreign securities which are now deposited with the Minister of Finance and for which they can easily find a market in the cities where their head offices are.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This discussion is out of order; but I should like to say, in answer to my hon. friend, that he has overlooked the fact that the deposits made by foreign companies are largely in Canadian investments, such as securities of municipalities and provinces, and mortgages.
Only partially.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think largely in Canadian securities.

What does the
Insurance Act require?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think it confines them to Canadian securities; but, as a matter of fact, the deposits made by these companies are largely in Canadian securities or mortgages.
Surely not mortgages?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Deposited with the Minister of Finance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, with trustees, because the Act provided for the deposit with the Minister of Finance or with trustees. Section 5 covers the case of deposits with a trustee or trustees. The suggestion of my hon. friend would mean that these companies would have to sell out their municipal and provincial securities and realize on their mortgages. That would be quite a serious disturbance; and, having regard to the situation as it exists, and the fact that our companies carry on business in foreign countries just as these companies carry on business in Canada, I think we have gone as far as it would be prudent to go.

I did not mean that
these foreign companies should be compelled to sell out their existing provincial or municipal securities. What I meant was that all foreign securities, which are now held by the Minister of Finance as a condition of these companies being permitted to do business, should be disposed of, and for them should be substituted securities of Canada. As a war measure, when we are making these exceptional provisions, there would be no harm in compelling that to be done.
I really think we should get the House in order. We are not in committee just yet. When this Bill goes into committee, this discussion will be in order.
Order. This discussion, although interesting, is absolutely out of order, and I would suggest that it take place in the Committee of the Whole.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and referred to the Select Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce.
The House again in Committee on Bill No. 37, to amend the White Phosphorus Matches Act.-Mr. Crothers. Mr. Rhodes in the Chair.	-
Is the minister satisfied that the Bill is all right as to form?

Yes.
On section 1-extension of time within which matches may be used:
This section repeals section 13 of the White Phosphorus Matches Act, what is that section?

It provides that the manufacture of these matches shall cease
on January 1, 1915, and that the sale shall cease on January 1, 1916. The effect of this section is to give six months longer to sell out the goods made prior to January 1, 1915, and also to extend the period within which such matches may be used to January 1, 1917. The chief object of the Bill was the protection of those in factories engaged in making these matches. The manufacture ceased at the date mentioned in the Bill, January 1, 1915, but a longer time is required to sell them, and those who buy require a longer time to use them. As the time allowed has expired, it is necessary to date this Bill back to January 1, 1916, which is done by section 2.
Mr. A. K. 'MACLEAN: What quantity of matches have they on hand?

I was given a statement of the number of cases, but have not it before me at the moment. They have on hand a considerable quantity, but they think they will be able to sell them out, in the usual course of business, within six months. My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) seemed to think there was something objectionable in the form of this Bill, but I cannot for the life of me see anything wrong in it. Section 1 provides that the original Act shall contain the wording here set forth. I think there is no - objection to the insertion of these words. Then, section 2 provides that the amendment proposed to the Act shall be deemed to have come into force on January 1, 1916. I cannot see that there is anything' contradictory in those two sections.

I have great respect for the view of my hon. friend, but I really would like to have his view confirmed by
the Minister of Justice, who is the legal adviser of the House. Section 1 repeals section 13 of chapter 12 of the Statutes of 1914, and substitutes the following:
This Act shall come into force on the first day of January, one thousand nine hundred and fifteen.
-except a certain section that is named. Then, section 2 provides:
The provisions of this Act shall he held to have come into force on, from and after the first dav of January, one thousand nine hundred and sixteen.

Not so far as the
original Act is concerned.

It does not say so. The result is that you first have a section of the old Act which is to come into force on January 1, 1915, and the Act that brings that

i
amending section into force does not itself become operative until a year afterwards, namely, January 1, 1916. If the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) says I am wrong in that, I have not a word to say.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The effect of section 1
of this Act is to provide that the Act of 1914 shall read as here provided instead of reading as it now does. It puts these words into the Act of 1914. In that case the words " this Act " apply to the Act of 1914, and in effect they are only a repetition of the words that presently are in the Act of 1914; for, as I understand it, the substantia] change is to add the proviso. If the Minister of Labour, instead of repealing the entire clause and substituting a new one, had proceeded by saying that this section of the Act of 1914 is amended by adding the following proviso, then section 14 would have read as it will read after this amendment is passed. I do not know whether I am mistaken or not, but it seems to me that the hon. gentleman's difficulty results from the fact that he takes the words " this Act " in the section it is proposed to substitute in the Act of 1914, and the words " this Act " in the second section of this Bill, as applying to the same Act, whereas, as a matter of fact, in the first place these words apply to the Act of 1914, and, in the second place, they apply to this Bill,- which will become an Act if it is passed. I do not see any contradiction here.

It is somewhat
confusing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I confess that until the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) made the suggestion, though I had read the Bill, it did not create any confusion in my mind.

Why are the words
"section 1 retroactive" put in the margin of section 2 of the Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand that to
refer to section 1 of this Bill being made retroactive, and the effect of that section is to amend the Act of 1914 so as to extend certain delays therein provided. I understand that the reason for making it retroactive is that under the existing disposition of the Act of 1914 offences have already been committed.
Unless this amendment is read as having dated back from the date mentioned in the second section, people might be affected, although we have changed the law now

and extended the time during which it was lawful to, do what they did.
Bill reported read the third time and passed.

Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 55, to amend the Winding-up Act.
He said: The purpose and effect of the Bill is simply to correct an anomalous situation that exists in the province of Ontario by reason of the fact that in the Winding-up Act "the court" is declared, for the province of Ontario, to mean the High Court of Justice of Ontario. To "the court" is committed the authority to make rules. Under the present arrangement of the courts in Ontario, there is one court called the Supreme Court of Ontario which has two divisions, the appellate division and the high court division. The result of the present (legislation is that, for the purpose of the Winding-up Act, the power of making rules is conferred upon the High Court of Ontario, and, under the general statute made at the time of the change of name, would pass exclusively to the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Ontario. All -other rules of practice in Ontario are made by the judges composing the entire Supreme Court of Ontario, the two divisions. It is represented by them that it is anomalous that we should have this exceptional case under the Winding-up Act, where the rules are made by the judges of one division only.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, considered in committee, reported, read the third time, and passed.
