Before going into the
items of the Department of Labour perhaps the minister would not mind if I should speak very briefly on the subject of shipbuilding in Canada to which I know my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), and otherhon. members have given a great deal of attention. This industry would, of course, give employment to a large number of labouring people, and in other ways it would prove of enormous advantage to Canada. I want to say, in the presence of the Minister of Labour and other members of the Government, who I

hope will give heed to my words-although the experience I have had in the past has not led me to hope for very much in that direction-that I think it is not only lamentable but is wholly discreditable to this Government that, although Canada has been engaged in this great war since August of 1914, upwards of 18 months, and although this Government has seen gradually disappearing the shipping of the Empire, and the shipping of Canada that in the past had a great deal to do with the carrying trade of Canada being commandeered by the British Government to meet the interests of the Empire; and although Canada was once one of the greatest shipbuilding countries in the world, this Government, so far as the public and this Parliament know, has not taken one single step during those 18 months towards the encouragement of shipbuilding in Canada.' The situation is getting worse. Only to-day we heard complaints by different members of the House 'as to difficulty in regard even to the getting of such a necessary article as coal from one part of our country to another. The situation is rapidly becoming worse, and it is a lamentable condition of affairs that this Government have not been able to see their way clear, up to this date, after the war has been in progress for 18 months, to announce to Parliament any measure which they have decided upon for the encouragement of shipbuilding in Canada. I can remember the time, not many years ago, when in the port of St. John, at the head of Courtenay bay, 1,200 men were employed in the building of ships; and all over the Maritime Provinces it was the same. We have great opportunities for shipbuilding upon, the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, and upon the Great Lakes, and all that our people need is reasonable encouragement to start up a great shipbuilding industry to give employment to thousands of our people. I would hope that to-day, in connection with the Estimates of the Department of Labour, the Minister will be able to give to this Parliament and the people of this country some hope that at last the Government has awakened to the necessity of taking hold of this important subject and is prepared to do something to restore to Canada this great industry which, not many years ago, was of such vast importance, and gave employment to so many people.

I think the bon. member for St. Joihn is quite right in more 102
i\ays than one. First of all, I think lie is right in expecting great things of this Government, and I think he is particularly right in expecting great things of the Minister of Labour. I am well aware that the Minister of Labour is very highly thought of by the people [DOT] of Canada, and that he has devoted his great industry and the best of his brilliant mind to the solution of various industrial difficulties in such a way as to meet -with the approval of the people in general and of labour in particular. The idea of encouraging industries is, of course, a protectionist idea, and naturally occurs to any reasonable man. It is absolutely in violation of all free trade principles. However, I am not here to chop logic on that question; I am here to agree with the 'hon. gentleman, and I think that the solution of one of the great difficulties of Canadian trade lies in that very encouragement to which he refers. There is at the present time before the United States Congress, a Bill of massive proportions for the encouragement, ot rather the restoration of the supremacy of American shipping. A friend of mine sent me a copy of it, which I promptly forwarded to the right hon. the Prime Minister, as it seemed to me to be not only of very great proportions but to contain within its four corners much that is of prime necessity to this continent in general. That Canada should have a merchant marine .is a prime necessity. We cannot hope for the lowering of freights unless we have a marine of our own which we can control.
I noticed a letter from the hon. gentleman in the press of this city a few days ago in which he urged the wisdom of having no imports.
I think the hon. gentleman has mistaken the import of the letter.
Will the hon. gentleman explain to me now what was in that letter?

I cannot offhand
because it was a reply.
What was the substance of it?

It was replying to a specific statement of a newspaper, and I am not aware that the newspaper took it up and repudiated it in the same
5 p.m. light that the hon. member for Halifax is anxious to do. I can not recall the letter as having any bearin on an objection to imports. It was specific statement which, if withdrawn

P aq

from its context and from the facts in dispute, might mean something altogether different. I am not prepared to undergo cross-examination on this point just now without at least having the letter here.

I understood the hon. member to say in that letter that it was very desirable from a Canadian standpoint that we should have no imports; and, if that was the hon. gentleman's view, I was going to ask him what he proposed to do with Canadian shipping.
I intended it for exports, that is all. I did not think anything about the imports at all; it was the exports.
So they would do business only the one way?
It did not occur to me that we were going to have a Canadian system of shipping for goods coming into Canada at all.
Just for exports?
And the ships would come back empty?

The point at issue was the matter of exchange, really, or the payment for goods in a particular way. It would be irregular, and I would be called( to order by the Chairman if I introduced that question here. As to that, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) is perfectly right. We are working in this coun-1 try under a great disadvantage, but by our genius and industry we hope to be able to export our goods to all- quarters of the globe. We should be provided with the means for export. .
How are we going to get paid for those exports?

That is a very elementary thing; I should think the hon. junior member for Halifax would work that out for himself if he would just take a little time'. That is a matter of political economy of a very simple sort.
How are we going to get the ships back? Will the Government have to pay something equivalent to freight to secure their return?
How are we going to get the ships back?
Yes. Is the hon. gentleman quite content that they should come back empty?
It is not likely that they will come back empty. They may make trips around the globe carrying other people's goods just as British ships do.

I can understand British ships doing that, because they carry the trade of every country in the world, and their ships can make trips to and from all parts of the world. It is not only that you are willing to export, but you want to know how you are going to get your ships back to this country under such, circumstances.

I can only say to the hon. gentleman that the principle of a free exchange of commodities which, he is endeavouring to introduce in this debate is entirely foreign to it. What I am arguing is that the preponderance of this country in trade and industry cannot be acquired by doing our manufacturing outside. It must be done here. The superiority of the Dominion is continually being demonstrated and it is an absolute denial of the contention that the hon. gentleman is now endeavouring to make. However, I agree heartily with the position taken by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) that we should aid, by every means in our power, the development of this as of every other industry.
Has the hon. gentleman any proposal to make as to how industries can assist the building of ships?
We might possibly imitate the free trade country which subsidizes its vessels and we might possibly develop the industry in that way.

We have a great many wounded men coming back from the front and we will have more. While these men have been loyal enough to volunteer to go to the front and fight for their country, I believe that they will be proud enough also when they come back to help themselves as much as possible by working for their own living. A great many will come back wounded and be unable to work at their ordinary vocations. At Lyons, France, they have already established large schools to educate wounded men. They are educating them in trades that they will be .able to work at no matter how badly they axe wounded, provided they are still capable of doing

something. By that means they will be able to make a living for themselves. I am quite sure, from what I know of a good many of the men who have gone to the front, that they would rather do that and be more or less independent than depend entirely on what they may get from the country in the way of an annuity. Now is the time, before too many of them come back, for the Minister of Labour to try to establish technical schools in various provinces where these men may be taught trades. The. expenses will probably be large, but not nearly so large as it would be to maintain the men in idleness. It is a step in the right direction, and now is the time to undertake it. I do not think we should wait until the war is over, because it always takes time to get anything of this kind properly started and under way. I would urge the minister to take up the question with his department at once, and try to work in conjunction with the various provinces to get the schools started. We have nothing of the kind in Canada as far as I know. The minister can easily get a description of the schools in France, and this would be of very material assistance to him in establishing them here. I understand that they are working admirably there and that the men are learning trades so that they will be in a position to help thehiselves which otherwise they could not do.

I want to support what my hon. friend from North Oxford has said in regard to the desirability of technical training for men partially disabled who have returned from the war. I had the honor of bringing that matter to the attention o'f the House on a former occasion and I can not allow the present occasion to pass without reinforcing what my hon. friend has said. I would like to ask the minister what department has charge of the care of returned soldiers. There is what is called, I think, a Hospital Commission, or something of the kind. Which minister is supposed to have charge of that commission?	-
Senator Lougheed is the chairman of it.
But I suppose it must be under some department answerable to Parliament.	[DOT]
I suppose it is under the Militia Department.

That is not the main point I want to speak of. Certainly, the education of partially disabled men is as important, not only to the men themselves, but to the welfare of the state, as anything else [DOT]that we can consider in connection with the war. We are going to have an enormous number of broken men, men who were .able to engage in the most active life before their enlistment. Otherwise, of course, they could not have enlisted. They are drawn from all walks of life. Some have toad educational opportunities; others have a trade; but a large proportion have not had any of these advantages. If these men are so disabled as not to be able to continue in tlhe vocations in which they were previously engaged, they may still be physically and mentally capable of engaging in other occupations suitable to their partially disabled condition; and it seems to me that we are not fully discharging our duty to these men unless, besides giving them their pensions, we give them an opportunity to acquire knowledge of one kind or another which they will be able to turn to advantage. A pension, let it be as liberal as you please, can never replace to the man himself the liberty and ability he had before he became disabled. Again, a citizen who is living on bis pension and engaged in no productive work, is not producing wealth for the State, or taking the part he could take if he were made competent according to his physical ability. It is only men who are entirely disabled, so to speak, or not of the brightest intellect, who cannot, by some form or other of education, be made efficient in some industrial or educational line. I think that this is a work that might very well be taken up 'by the department over which frny hon. friend presides. I can think of no other department of the Government within whose sphere it could more naturally or properly fall, and I therefore desire to support the suggestion of my hon. friend from North Oxford, and urge as strongly as I can that this is a duty which rests upon our country; an obligation which we can never fully discharge, but which, so far as we are able, we certainly should discharge, not only in the interests of the man himself, but in the interests of the state as well.
When the Prime Minister was discussing something in this connection on a previous occasion, I had the honour to mention to-the House that at the present moment

there is a technical school in the city of Edmonton fully equipped for this kind of work. The equipment is paid for by the Provincial Government, and the school is maintained at the cost of the tax-payers of the city, with some assistance from the Provincial Government. Here, right at hand, we have an institution that would cover the case in a very considerable measure. There are men in the school for teaching quite a number of trades. The school is conveniently situated for taking care of a large number of returned soldiers. I did not urge this upon the Government when I mentioned the matter before; but I do urge upon the attention of the Minister of Labour now, and through him upon the attention of the Government, that this school be utilized. Already we have a large number of partially disabled soldiers in Edmonton and Northern Alberta; men who have served their country to the best of their ability, and are now broken men. Owing to financial conditions, there is a possibility of the school at Edmonton being closed, o,r at all events/ of its scope and efficiency being largely reduced. And I would very strongly urge that instead of waiting any longer, the Government might very well begin to experiment in this matter by taking cognizance of this particular school, and adopting means whereby co-operation can be secured between this' Government and the school authorities; or, if the Government thought fit, they could take entire charge of the school with a view to the education, in such trades and callings as the men are physically fitted for, of those partially disabled soldiers who have returned from the front and are willing to engage in those callings.
It will be understood that the disabled man who is desirous of attending such a school must have means of support while he is receiving instruction; that is a matter that would have to be considered, and if it were taken care of, it would have to be at the expense of the Dominion Government. That would be supplementary to the soldier's pension, which, of course, would not be sufficient to enable him to attend the school and support himself. I would not advocate that men should be put in this school to learn trades that they are not mentally fitted for, or that they should be forced into any school. But a labourer, for instance, who has had no opportunity of learning a trade, and has lost a leg, we will say, might learn at tljds school some trade that he could become absolutely efficient in without his full complement of legs. But
[Mr. Oliver.!
in order to enable him to do that somebody would have to supplement his pension. If the man were ambitions and mentally fitted for the work, I think it would be a most excellent investment for the Government of the country from every point of view. Besides, I maintain that it is a legitimate obligation that properly rests upon us to see that everything that can be done is done to make up to those men the loss that they have suffered and the loss which the state has suffered by reason of the reduced efficiency of these citizens. I therefore take this opportunity of urging upon the Government, and upon the Minister of Labour, in whose department this matter most properly falls, and who has in a large measure the organization at his disposal, the necessity of giving effect to the suggestions I have made. I hope that it will be possible for him to see the matter as I have tried to present it to the House, and that he will present it to his colleagues successfully, so that we may have results, and I wish particularly to put in a word for the technical school at Edmonton, which stands there to-day ready and prepared to do this work.

The question of technical education comes home acutely to a great many people on account of the situation presented in Canada by the lack of occupation for our returned soldiers. That situation naturally calls for sympathy and attention of an unusual kind, but that does not in any way lessen the general importance and necessity of Canada taking some forward step in regard to the whole question of technical education. When we contemplate, as we have been doing during the past few months, the return to Canada of men who might be classed as broken men with all their old affiliations and associations, formed previous to their going to the front, broken off, and a new phase of life opened up to them, it is natural that we should look to the state to provide some certainty of occupation for those men on their return. In regard to the whole question of pensions, I have on the Order Paper a motion on which I hope to address the House in a few days, but in regard to the duty of Canada to our returned soldiers, I wish to make some remarks now, because last summer in my own province the attention of the Government was called to its duty in this connection. The Hospitals Commission, which was appointed by the Government and over which Senator Loug-heed presides, is composed of a large number of estimable gentlemen throughout

Canada n'ot directly connected with the Government, who are anxious to serve in some way and who have, no doubt, given a great deal of service on that commission. It occurred to a number of people in our province that what is known as technical or vocational training in connection with our returned soldiers was the fundamental solution of the problem after they had been [DOT] brought through the stages of illness and convalescence. That problem was presented last summer in my province to the commission, and a large amount of correspondence was carried on with Mr. Seammell, secretary of the commission; and, although I am not making any announcement on the part of the commission, I understand they appreciate to the full the desirability and the necessity of some action being taken in that regard. At a conference held between the members of the commission and the representatives of the different provincial governments, a plan for vocational training was submitted by Professor Sexton, who is at the head of the technical schools at Halifax, and the method of training under provincial and federal control was adopted and approved by that body. I have under my hand a letter from the head of one of the technical schools, and, as it is interesting in tips connection and show's what has been done, I will read it to the House:
We have already admitted several returned men to this school, and, as I intimated to you in conversation when you visited the school last December, we find ourselves well equipped to give Just the help the men need. These men have been admitted without fee on the expectation that the ultimate arrangements made by the Dominion Government will include a sufficient grant to relieve our Board of Education from the additional expenditure.
That, I think, is the crux of the matter at this stage.
The expense connected with this work will be greater for each indiivdual than that required for the care of the average pupil in regular attendance at the school. The classes for soldiers will of necessity be smaller, a greater variety of work will be presented, and the work itself must be more intensive, requiring the highest grade of skilful industrial teachers. However, I am confident that with the co-operation of our Advisory Industrial Committee and the Board of Education, which is assured, and with a sufficient grant to cover the additional expense, we can provide in our new building for the teaching of several hundred of these men. There is no doubt in my mind as to the necessity of providing this work. Let me give you two examples:
1. A young man, not yet 19 years of age, who had formerly been connected with this school, has returned with loss of one eye ar.ll with a badly maimed left arm. He is now being prepared for matriculation into the Faculty of Applied Science of the University of Toronto, and will ultimately become a civil engineer.
2. A young Scotchman, age 27, who has had some experience in railroad work, and whose right arm is partially paralysed, is being taught railroad telegraphy. He has had a fair elementary education, and will become, I expect, a proficient man in the line of work chosen.
Several have been inquiring about taking work with us, and I find it a little early yet for them in their period of convalescence. But now that the men are returning in large numbers, it seems desirable to formulate some definite plan, and to make it widely known.
That illustrates the practicability of the proposition suggested, and the way in which it is being worked out. It is recognized by the different bodies who have been consulted that the situation is this: Technical education being under the control of the provinces, there are already in Nova Scotia, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Alberta and British Columbia, technical schools with varied equipment depending on their age and the conditions in the respective provinces, which are prepared to take in pupils for vocational training. In my province there was established a few years ago by tlie Provincial Government a magnificent school, which is doing splendid work and by which the soldiers from the Maritime Provinces may be fitted for new vocations in place of those for which their experience at the front has. to tally unfitted them. In Toronto, there is a magnificent school which was opened only last year, and which is equipped as well as almost any technical school on this continent.
Under whose control is it?
It is under the control of the city of Toronto. In Montreal the technical school is equally well equipped.
There are two of them in Montreal.

And my hon. friend from Edmonton speaks of the conditions in that town. It seems to me that assistance in vocational training must come from the Dominion Government and that it ought really to form part of our war expenditure. I do not wish to enter upon any controversial subject in regard to a matter of this kind as to which there is no party feeling, although I realize that there are items comprising millions of dollars which are to be included in our war debt, which certainly deserve to be investigated; but I feel that it would be proper to include in our war debt any sum necessary to provide vocational training for our returned soldiers and to equip the young men of this country

to aid in the industrial development of Canada, That money 'has to be found, and I realise the difficulty of finding it out of the ordinary revenues of the country; but I submit that the proper place to find it is out of the war debt of the country, because the necessity for this work is a direct consequence of the war. Tentative arrangements have 'been made, in certain provinces at least, under which men who have returned, and who 'are in a convalescent stage in some of the homes which exist in certain of the different provinces, are being trained, and in my province the provincial authorities are preparing to provide technical instruction in the vicinity of those homes in order that education along technical' lines may be given to those men as soon as they are able to receive it.
That cannot be done without money. The Provincial Governments provide the schools and the instructions; it is the duty of this country to assume, as part of the burden imposed by the war, the responsibility of providing education for these men. In the working out of this problem, the necessity suggested by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) would be provided for. But I go further and say that this is a duty imposed upon this country as a whole as a direct result of the war and because of the conditions which will exist in Canada by reason of the war. I find the following in the report of the Department of Labour:
While the importance of the whole subject of technical education is unquestioned, the pressing urgency of other matters consequent on the outbreak of war has not made the past year opportune for further action.
I say that the duty of increasing the opportunities of technical education falls upon us as a direct consequence of the war; it is just as much the duty of those responsible for the direction of Canada's affairs as is the sending of men to the front.
More so.

My hon. friend is
more emphatic on the point than I have stated. The duty is imperative and the necessity for action equally so.
What is the situation? We are taking men between eighteen and forty-five years of age, wherever we can find them; asking them to go voluntarily and fight the battle of the Empire and of civilization. The Prime Minister has 'intimated that the aim of Canada is to send half a million men. Realizing the situation and the necessity, the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, speaking yesterday in Montreal in the 
presence of the Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) pointed out what it means to the industrial life of this country to take away half a million men. He spoke as one enthusiastic and sympathetic for Canada performing her full duty in the war. In my own province, in the great coal industry, from 1,500 to 2,000 men engaged in mining have gone to the front. These are men in the most active period of their lives. They are leaving the old men, who were loaders of the coal, and the 'boys, who have 'been doing boys' work. The consequence is that coal production is seriously interfered with. To-day we heard the complaint made by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean), and I have myself voiced the complaints of industries in Nova Scotia, including those engaged in the manufacture of munitions, that the reduced coal production is impairing their efficiency. This is only one line of industry, but in every other line something of the same result is seen by reason of the fact that the men in the prime of life have been taken away, leaving the older men and the boys. A large percentage of these men will come back, as the hon. member for Edmonton has said, broken men. How are you going to prepare the boys to handle the technical work that these men have been doing?
But that is not all. When you look at what Canada is to be, when you hear our optimists talk about the great immigration that will come to Canada from other countries, the question is, how are we to equip ourselves to 'build up the industrial prosperity which: Canada must have if she is to fulfil her high destiny? You are taking away the very flower of our industrial army. The only way to supply the places of those who have gone is to fit the boys early to fill the places of the others. This is a necessity resting upon the Dominion as a whole, as a direct consequence of the war. Consider what was done in Germany. I do not often quote at length, but I have a statement here which puts the case so clearly, and with such emphasis, that, perhaps, I may be pardoned if I read it:
When industrial evolution progressed to such a state that the apprenticeship system began to seriously weaken, Germany bethought herself of providing trade instruction in the schools. The master workman was so busy maintaining themselves against the competition of others and in keeping up with the scientific advancement of his trade that he did not have time to teach the apprentice. The latter found that his branch of industry was being so minutely specialized by the division of labour that he did not have a chance to acquire all the fundamentals of his vocation in his master's workshop. Schools were started which offered prac-

lli&i
tical training suitable for various trades in the evenings and on Sundays. At first attendance at these classes was voluntary, but when it came to be recognized that the instruction was immensely valuable to both wage-earners and employers, compulsory attendance was introduced and has become almost universal in Germany. It became evident that evening and Sunday classes were too great a strain upon the young'workers, so that later developments have made it necessary for employers to allow their apprentices free time in working hours to attend school for six to eight hours a week and pay them at the same rate as if they were working in the factory. Some manufacturers opposed these regulations for a year or more and then supported such measures because they found the training and increased intelligence of the workers was more advantageous to their output than if the young men were kept all the time in the factory. Thus it Is seen that the state has the boy under Its control in tha schools after he has gone to work and almost up to the age of maturity. If he goes to work at 14 he has to continue in the special industrial schools for either three or four years more until he becomes a journeyman. The extent of these schools may be judged from the number who attend in the kingdom of Prussia. In 18S4 there were 58,000 pupils enrolled in these industrial schools, and in 1909, the number had increased to 360,000.
The extent of the instruction in different trades may be comprehended when one realizes that in the city of Munich 52 different trades are provided for by separate teachers and schools. There are classes for such apprentices as hotel waiters, chimney-sweeps, plasterers, blacksmiths, bakers, saddlers, and men in other callings which we consider do not need any theoretical training to learn their trade. This city of 580,000 people spends nearly $250,000 a year on this kind of teaching alone.
Besides training competent mechanics Germany provides schools for preparing bosses and foremen. Men who have been through the industrial schools and have worked at their trade for two or more years may go to institutions where they spend most of their time for two or three years in receiving instruction to prepare themselves for positions of industrial responsibility lower than those of manager. These thoroughly trained men superintend and direct the operations of journeymen in Germany's factories.
This progressive country also provides splendid technical colleges for the training of engineers, commercial universities for the preparation of men who shall direct the business and industry of the empire, navigation schools, mining schools, industrial art schools, leather schools, textile schools, etc. There is some sort of education offered for every kind of human activity and every grade or worker. The older traditional education is not slighted and generous provision is made for classical education in public schools and universities. There is an absolute faith among all the people in the power for good education and everywhere honour is accorded to any kind of trained man commensurate with this degree of learning.
Is it any wonder that Germany has forged to the forefront of civilized nations in the last 30 or 40 years? In 1870 the manufactures, the inventions and the foreign commerce of the separate German states were far below those of England and France. To-day united Germany stands in the front rank of the nations of the world in industrial production and she clearly
leads all other nations in the application of science to the industry and to the arts. Her position is all the more remarkable because this result has been achieved in a country in which the agricultural and mineral resources are not great and In the face of the burdens due to long and costly wars, to maintenance of a great army and to the draining of a large part of its population through emigration. Where the emigration in the 80's was 200,000 a year, it is now only 25,000, who go mostly to South America and Africa, where German industrial projects are being carried out. The Germans themselves are proud to proclaim that the greatest single instrument in accomplishing their wonderful industrial growth has been technical education.	.
A few years ago, a number of prominent German manufacturers, educationists and public men made an extensive tour in the United States with the idea of finding out how serious a competition the latter nation might prove in the future struggle for world trade. Their concensus of opinion was that the United States possessed greater natural resources, a superior factory system, workmen of greater energy, industry, and mechanical skill and cheaper railway transportation. Notwithstanding all these advantages, the German experts thought that even the existing grip of America on international trade would tend to weaken. They commented on the absence of any adequate system of special education for commerce, banking or foreign trade in the United iStates. The meagreness of technical education, the trifling annual contingent of chemists, engineers, trained foremen, educated dyers, weavers, electricians, and mechanics as compared with the throng of lawyers, physicians, dentists and unspecialized graduates of colleges seemed shortsighted and improvident. The foreign investigators concluded that on the whole the "American danger" had been greatly exaggerated, and that a steadfast adherence by Germany to the technical educational policy and commercial methods now in practice will leave the fatherland little to fear in future competition with American manufactured goods.
This condition in Germany, the existence of which is conceded on all sides, is the result of thirty years' development along the lines of technical education. Why is it that Germany to-day possesses so many trade secrets? The processes connected with dyeing trades are known only to Germany. Large amounts of money are being expended in some parts of the United States for the purpose of inquiring into these processes with a view to establishing the dyeing industry in that country. Why is it that Germany possesses these secrets? Simply because their young men were educated along scientific lines. Why is it that ordinary German soldiers are able to manipulate the instruments by the use of which they employ what we are inclined to call nefarious and inhuman systems of warfare? Simply because the common men over there learned all these things as part of their early training and education.

Our newspapers keep pointing out to the people in an optimistic way the benefits that will come to Canada after the war. There are people who say, " We are going to have so many people on the land." All right; let us have the people on the land. But our country will not develop as enormously as is hoped for if the population is confined to the land. We must have those who till the soil and produce the wheat, but we must take steps along these other lines as well if we hope to obtain the development in this country that we want. During the last fifteen years there has been' a tendency on the part of the people to go from the country into the towns. It is just as important to Canada that the people who come to our cities shall be trained to be useful, producing citizens, as it is to have men on our farms producing wheat.
The necessity of some action in this regard seems to me to be absolutely imperative. I am not speaking in a partisan way; I simply desire to impress upon the minister and upon the Government the necessity for some Action. I might make complaints; I might indulge in unfavourable criticism; but I do not purpose doing that, because I think the subject ought to be dealt with along broad lines.
It may be said that education is a matter that should be looked after by the provinces. What has been done in this regard? A few days ago we voted an immense sum of money to be used over a period of ten years for the education and instruction of young men along agricultural lines. Schools have been erected in provinces where formerly they did not exist; arrangements have been made with the provincial authorities for the expenditure of this money every year, with a view to extending the facilities of agricultural instruction. Assistance is given to two schools interested in subjects connected with navigation. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has made provision for navigation schools in connection with the technical schools in our province; these navigation schools are doing good work. Assistance has been given to McGill university for a transportation course and for a forest-products laboratory; assistance has been given in a number of other ways. The constitutional question, therefore, does not present any difficulty at all; the Provincial and Federal Governments have worked together in the expenditure of this [DOT]51,000,000 which we give every year to agrioulture.

It may be said that a proposal of this kind involves extravagant expenditure at a time when we ought to economize.	But, hon. gentlemen,
remember the old scriptural saying, " there is that scattereth, and yet increaseth ; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty." It is a peculiar thing to me if hon. gentlemen cannot find in the Estimates that [DOT] have been brought down to Parliament any sum of money which could be taken out and a substitution made therefor of a sum to be devoted to the assistance of technical education. In our province some of the citizens have offered bursaries to stimulate educational competition among the younger men, with the result that during the last year or two young men have been able to take up short courses at the technical schools and fit themselves for active industrial work. But necessarily that comes within the scope of the duty of the State. The results are by no means so broad or comprehensive as could be obtained or as ought to be obtainedby that generous assistance which this Government should be able to give. It seems to me that satisfactory results could be obtained by the application of federal assistance to the organization that we have in Canada to-day in the matter of technical education. No grants should be made or assistance given for the purchase of sites or the erection of buildings; provision for these should be made by the provinces. But supplementary assistance ought to come from this Government for maintenance, for development, and for the special equipment which is necessary in order to provide for the soldiers who will return from the war and for the men who must take the places of those who have gone to the front. With some support of that kind, having the educational facilities in all the towns where we have manufacturing interests, there is no reason why the local boards of education should not provide for technical instruction along certain lines. Certain cities in Ontario, I understand, are now taking steps towards beginning this work.

Night schools are the
germ of that.

Night schools in the cities. Hamilton and London are two
cities-
But they do not go far enough with the type of education that will suit the returned maimed soldiers.

The returned maimed soldier is only the smallest part of the problem. He can be and will be provided for. My argument is that the public are only beginning to appreciate the serious necessity of grappling with this problem on seeing the object lesson of the returned soldiers. I can understand that the public are apt to be quiescent upon this problem. I think the minister will agree that arrangements have already been made for some institutions to deal with the returned soldiers. But where you have the technical institutions in the particular provinces, and where you have the provincial authorities in sympathy with you, the problem can be worked out.
I was advised by Prof. Sexton, only a week ago, when he was here in attendance at the meeting of the Mining Institute, that they were proceeding to send two or three instructors to a convalescent home in my province to begin instruction in the different trades which these men might be suitable for. He thought the first thing to do was to have experts who were accustomed to training people to vocations, to determine what the men who had come back from the front could do, and what lines of usefulness they could be trained in, so as to supply education along that particular line. We are only beginning to awaken to the necessity of action "on the question of technical education generally, by reason of the fact that we see these disabled men coming back from the front. We know that they have nothing to do, and the question is, what are we going to do with them? Hence technical education comes to the front.

Speak-. ing of the duty of the Government in regard to technical education, it was quite understood that the question of the care of the returned soldiers is to be in charge of the Hospital Commission; and, as was said before dinner, the understanding is that the provinces will provide the facilities for the educational training of any of these men, with assistance to be given by the Federal Government through the Hospital Commission. But I have already pointed out that the arrangements for carrying this into effect have not been perfected. I assume, however, that they will be perfected. Should this not be accomplished, the responsibility for failure will rest upon the Government.
That, however, is only one of the phases of the larger question. In regard to that larger question, Canada seems to be living very much in the present. We are concerned, indeed obsessed, with the task that has come to us of taking part in the war, and

of enlisting all our people within the ages when volunteering could be expected. Occasionally, an optimist like the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) tells us of the many thousands of people who are coming here after the war, and this very splendid condition of affairs is expected as a matter of certainty simply because many of our people do not stop to think about the real question, the question whether we are equipped to achieve the results that we desire. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) spoke some warning words in regard to the situation and reminded us of our duty, a duty which I am attempting in some small way to recall to the attention of the House and the country. The hon. gentleman said:
It would toe a great mistake if we put away from us all care, all investigation, all fronting of what will toe the real difficulties 'of the future, and that when the supreme economic struggle comes And ourselves not well prepared, light-heartedly and without thorough examination entering into the greatest contest in our history, the greatest in the history of the world.
And in concluding his remarks upon that portion of the subject he said:	_
Looking at the matter in that light, we cannot look forward to the end of the war and keep ourselves up until that period on the false assumption that peace will "bring with it unexampled prosperity.
I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce was not too pessimistic. Thousands, and hundreds of thousands, of the very flower of our country's life will come home disabled, with their ambitions of life gone, many of them unfitted for the occupations in which they were engaged before the war. This will impose upon the rest of the Canadian people the task of caring for these men. Our population, in proportion to our area, is a comparatively sparse one, and when you take the spirit and ambition of the energetic men between 18 and 45 from the life of this country, and impair the usefulness ol many of these men, the problem that awaits the Canadian people is seen to be a very serious one. And that problem is not helped by declaring that we are to have a tremendous immigration upon our agricultural lands. After the battle upon the plains of Europe and the East is over, will come the great industrial contest, in which the maintenance of our interests will depend upon our being in a position to grasp a portion of the world's trade. Where are we to find the men to fill the places of those who have been taken from the industrial life of this country-and not
merely the places that are now empty, but those that must be created if Canada is to become the nation she ought to be? Today our eyes are blinded to the real industrial situation by the fictitious prosperity created by the injection into the business life of the country of an expenditure of three or four hundred millions upon munitions of war. Many industries which were absolutely in a state of quiescence before this expenditure began are now active. We do not realize the conditions which the Minister of Trade and Commerce has shown as inevitably coming. But the question of how to prepare for this coming condition is one worthy the most serious attention of this House. We might well lay aside many of the petty squabbles in which we engage to devote ourselves to this question.
Hear, hear.

That is not to say that the loyal Opposition in this free Parliament should allow hon. gentlemen opposite to assume a Kaiser-like attitude. It does not mean that, because the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) and his associates come to Parliament and indicate their will, we, the representatives of a free people, are bound ^to accept it, nor that these hon. gentlemen are to be above criticism.
Who is objecting?

The hon. member's method of objecting may take one form or it may take another. If I am to understand him as agreeing that we should devote ourselves to the consideration of the great question which I am discussing, I would accept his position frankly. What I complain of is that the Government has not devoted itself to the question of where Canada is to find herself at the end of this war. The hon. Minister of Public Works knows that. He knows that the president of the Canadian Pacific railway found it necessary, only yesterday, to raise objection to certain methods of the Government in that regard.
Was it only yesterday that he raised that question?

So far as I know from reading the papers, he made a public utterance on that question yesterday. Of course, he may have been talking to my

hon. friend privately; if so, I suppose my hon. friend can tell us all about it.
Oh, no; he never talked to me privately.

I do not want to be diverted from the consideration of the matter which I am in all seriousness endeavouring to present to the House, solely with the idea of attempting to convince hon. gentlemen of its importance and of the necessity of dealing with it along big and broad lines. The consideration of the question as to where Canada is to be after this war may well occupy the larger share of our attention, because it is the supreme question affecting the Canadian people at this time. The future destiny of Canada is not to be eolved simply by declaring that immigration is to take place, or that this, that, or the other thing is to occur. We must deliberately, clearly and calmly analyze the economic condition of the country, see what changes >are necessary, see what preparation should be made, and 'endeavour to meet the condition which we know is to come. To-day in Canada we have colleges for the education of our pro- [DOT] feseional men; we have schools where our boys and girls are taught the rudimentary elements of education; we have agricultural schools, which receive encouragement and assistance from Federal and Provincial Governments. With the exception of the action taken in the matter of technical education by the provinces,
' which have strained their revenues to the limit in dealing with the problem, no action has been taken to provide for the training of our artisans in such manner that we in Canada shall be able to make things that we do not now make, and to make better those things which we do make at the present time. If we in this Parliament can do anything to attain that end, we shall be fulfilling in some measure our duty in this respect. In the province of Nova Scotia the advantages derived from assisting technical education have been demonstrated. Some twenty years ago mining schools were established in the province, in which men who worked in the mines could study in the evenings those things a knowledge of which would make them more efficient in their work. The result is that to-day it is our proud boast that the managerial positions in all our mines are filled by the sons of Nova Scotia, who were trained in these local technical schools. But outside of the local technical schools that are to be found 
in one or two places in the country, no organized attempt has been made to follow out a systematic method of technical education. 1 hope that it will be possible for the Minister of Labour to initiate at this session of Parliament some comprehensive and systematic method of training, in the application of technical education, the younger men of this country who are not going to the war. The marvels of the science of chemistry have been a potential factor in the development of this country; they should be put in the possession of the intelligent young people of Canada so that they may deal with them, elaborate them, and derive from them the results which have been obtained in Germany. Now is the time to begin. It will not do to begin this work after the war-that will be too late. The advantages which may be obtained in the way of trade, business, and other conditions, will all be pre-empted by other countries when the world gets right again, unless we begin now. The report of my hon. friend's department intimates that during the war a barrier to progress in this respect is encountered in a financial sense. I submit that that is not a barrier. If you deal with the problem of the vocational training of the soldier who returns from the war, you will take the money out of the war debt. Assistance to technical education in the different provinces would be just as much a charge upon the war debt as any expenditure for munitions or anything else that you buy for war purposes. You do the one thing in order that the Canadian boys can go out and win; if you do the other, you provide for a situation for which the war is directly responsible. I trust that I have not pressed this question along lines which will prove unacceptable to my hon. friend the minister. Canada's duty in this matter has always appealed to me as being one of the very highest importance. I have offered these remarks in no spirit of partisanship or of hostility to the Government; I present them as opening up a line of action for this Government upon which they should embark without delay.

I think the committee will agree that the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. E. M. Macdonald) has presented the case of technical education with a great deal of honest fervour and enthusiasm. The speech that he has made is one of those series of observations which go a long way in encouraging those people who have so vast an undertaking as this in their

hands. There was a time when the universe at large, more particularly what we understand now by nature, was a closed book. It is only one hundred years since it was first known that there was a mysterious substance called phlogiston in wood and in other combustible substances, which, when warmed to a sufficient degree of heat, liberated itself and caused the consumption of the wood. When it was discovered that it was the combination of oxygen with the constituents of the wood-or fuel, or whatever it might be-at a certain temperature which provided this astonishing result, the natural cause of the phenomenon burst upon the world at large, and the science of chemistry was founded. That was one hundred years ago. Since that time there has developed every conceivable form of natural and scientific curiosity. Each has rewarded the sons of men with the most extraordinary results, not the least of these being the science of hydrostatics or the dynamics of electrical science. All These things now provide the casual reading of men who a few years ago did not know anything about them. Our libraries now contain books of so clear and specific and, definite a character that any man or woman who has a reasonable degree of curiosity can take those books and read the romance of nature, which in terms may seem to be a contradiction, but which, as a matter of fact, is the most wonderful thing in the history of the universe. It is only a few years since people, some, indeed, now lingering upon the scene, looked up at the skies without knowing what they meant. It is only a few years since the matter of discovering, the constituent elements of sirius, the dog-star, flashed upon the world.; when Kirkhoff and Bernstein, following up Sir Isaac Newton's wonderful discovery of the spectroscope, produced the sprectrum analysis, when at once all those materials which go to make up this globe were discovered to be in the stars and in the suns that fill the vastness of space. The consequence was that mankind learned to realize the wonderful unity that exists, not only according to the laws of gravitation and movement, but according to the eopernican law, in all of those wonderful things connected with what might be called particularly the science of mechanics. As soon as all those wonderful things were seen, the unity of the qualities and constituents of the stars, the riddle of the universe was read. We have come down now to the time when the electron, that single vortex of force which so long ago was foreshadowed by Nervton and later
on by Lord Kelvin to be the ultimate constituent of matter, has been ascertained to be the necessarily ultimate constituent of matter. The unity of force and matter has been established. Force and matter for many a long generation were considered, to be two things; in fact, it was a great discovery when force was defined to be a condition of matter; but now they are ascertained to be one and the same thing. So that we have at last got down to the basis of all things, and when people at large understand this and are able to grasp the simple, great, overpowering and overwhelming fact that law, comprising a variety of laws, is the basis of the method and the matter of the universe, all the rest is comparatively simple, a matter of detail, and immediately becomes within the sphere of general knowledge.	,
Mankind was a wonder until the cell was discovered; and when the whole of the living world was discovered to depend on the ultimate constituent of the cell, when the cellular theory was outlined, humanity and all of nature become somewhat different. The inorganic and the organic world might then be related, and it was found that they were. At last it dawned on some inquiring mind that the crystal was alive -and then was bridged the apparent chasm between the organic [DOT] and the inorganic worlds. This inquiring spirit has raised the enthusiasm of mankind. Those men who for long years worked for an insufficient amount of money from early morning till late at night in a vague and precarious and hazardous endeavour to maintain their families and bring them up intellectually, are appealing to the world to be at least provided with the means of acquiring knowledge-not with the mere reward of toil, with wages. There is not a workman, an artisan, a mechanic, in the world who at the present time is not a professional man in the highest and the most dignified sense. These men are now working with an understanding of the principles of knowledge and the principles of construction, and doing this, there is no finer body of intellect or occupation in the world. Such a work as we are engaged in-mere administration, stained frequently by the vehemence and sins of politics-fades into insignificance beside their works. These men are the apostles of the great future, built upon their understanding of an infinitely great past. That in my opinion 9 p.m. is why the Classics have gone. At one time they ruled the world. If a man could jabber a little bit of Latin,

he was a wonder. If a man had a son who knew the difference between amo and canto, or some simple thing like that, he immediately proceeded to edify his neighbours by bragging about it, and frequently quoted a lot of Latin that never existed and that was forbidden by all the rules of syntax or prosody. But that made no difference,
And still the wonder grew,
That one small head could carry all he knew.
But that day has gone by. People are not frightened a bit now either by the sound of a dead language or by stupidity and superstition. They have worked their way into the uncommon nature of things and they have become imbued with this lofty spirit of knowledge. When I meet a man who understands what he is doing in the construction or the manipulation of steel, I, being only a lawyer, take my hat off to him. There was a time when I would have thought, not knowing any better, that if anybody was going to take off his hat he would be the man; but not now, that day has gone by. The mere cut-and-dried professions are nothing; it is the inquirer after knowledge to whom we have to look; and therefore, when we conduct ourselves in so sordid and mean a way as to pay vulgarly low and insufficient wages for the knowledge that these men have acquired and for the highly spiritual manner in which they apply it, and when we consider that their families are entitled to the best and are ready to take the best and ready to develop the best that we can afford, it becomes indescribably mean when we pay large sums to the grafters and vulgar manipulators of ordinary every-day life. The sin then becomes vastly greater, and, to tell you the truth, I can quite understand why it is that a man has written a book in which he says it is a sin and a shame to die rich; and the time will no doubt come when it will be considered a reproach to a man not to know enough to employ his money in the spread of knowledge- that such a man has not acquired the first element of knowledge, and we may rest assured that his mind and his taste are both equally vulgar and uncultivated.
And what about these schools?

If I have failed to show you why it is that these schools are necessary, and why it is that their time has arrived, then my remarks have been in vain. I had hoped that I would have imbued gentlemen like yourself with that enthusi-

astic spirit which I at this moment feel for the acquirement of knowledge by one and all. That is why I introduced the subject in this way. I will leave its further dis-cusion to other men, like the hon. gentleman from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), who has so ably demonstrated the necessity of pursuing this matter with all industry and skill, and to the minister himself. I felt that perhaps there was something incumbent upon me to say which might induce or develop in us all that spirit of enthusiasm which itself is the very spark of freedom and of knowledge.
That it is which drives us on to higher and nobler things, for I am thoroughly impressed with this idea, that once your son ot your daughter has acquired a taste for real knowledge, there is nothing under God's heaven that can stop them except their last breath. It is a habit. It is a wonderful thing; but it is a habit that once acquired can never be given up. It is the only good habit I know of that is like that. But it is a fact, and therefore, if we can do anything, by word of mouth or in any other way, to induce others who are less skilled perhaps than we are to enter upon this way of knowledge and pursue it but for a short time, we can rest assured of one thing, and that is that they will never be able to forsake it. There is no going back; there is no apostasy. Disease, physical corruption, may overtake man or woman, but the spirit-the divine spirit- of knowledge, and love of knowledge, the breadth and singleness of purpose which true knowledge gives, which we see every day exemplified in scientific men who give up their priceless discoveries to the world at large without qualms or selfseeking, endure forever. If these men were politicians they would start dickering over every little thing-the invention of some contrivance to latch a door, or something of that sort; but that is not the divine spirit of knowledge. Once the divine breath of knowledge enters a man, he is spiritually regenerated, and, if at any time, fit for the Kingdom of Heaven. I know that the minister is imbued with this spirit of enthusiasm, and I pay him no idle compliment to-day when I say I know that, because I know many of the leading representatives of labour in this country, and they feel that he has their interests at heart. If I did not think he had their interests at heart I frankly would not pay him the deference of saying this,

but I think it, and I believe they think it too. Theie are other people, no doubt. I do not wish to derogate from the good qualities of anybody who has gone before.' I know that the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) was a man inspired with the desire to benefit the working men and develop their knowledge. It does no man any good to deprive another,of his just meed of praise. Before I sit down let me say-and I cannot express myself too strongly in this regard-that we must devote ourselves more than ever to the enthusiasm which underlies the acquirement of knowledge, and we can rest assured that if we do the people will 'be only too glad to acquire it.

Mr. Chairman, I desire to make a
few observations on this subject. There is in the House and in the country very little difference of opinion as to the desirability and need of lending our assistance to education in all its branches. I do not think that I go astray when I say that last week this House committed itself in a sense to the principle of technical education in accepting my resolution and approving of the methods that this Government has adopted to develop the flax industry of this country. I do not think that we have any reason to look farther for an example of the results to be obtained from technical education than the work which has been accomplished under the direction of the Department of Agriculture in the different counties throughout Ontario and, I understand, in other provinces. I think no better evidence of the interest which this Government has taken in the question of technical education could be afforded than the fact that in the distribution of the agricultural grants authorized by this Parliament provision was made that a liberal proportion of the money should be expended in the further development of agricultural education and instruction. Prior to the time when this system of imparting agricultural instruction in the various counties was adopted, we had our agricultural colleges in the provinces and our experimental farms in the Dominion, and young men from the farms were getting the benefit of the instruction that the teachers at the colleges and farms could impart. What was the result when they had acquired this knowledge? In only a very limited number of cases did the men who had taken advantage of these educational opportunities go back to the farm
to apply their knowledge to useful purpose in their own districts, but, on the other hand, the brightest and best of the men graduates from these colleges became instructors in the colleges and on the experimental farms of foreign countries and sister colonies. We would be in exactly the same position, from a medical point of view, if our doctors and medical men, after graduating from the universities 'and colleges of our country, ceased to prosecute their profession in our midst and gave to other lands the benefit of their study and experience. Under such circumstances, of what earthly use would they be to us? I may be drifting away somewhat from the subject before the committee at the present time, but I refer to this for the reason that our Government has awakened to the fact that if we let the brightest of our men get away from us, instead of devoting their education to the upbuilding of their own country, thd money spent upon their instruction will have been practically wasted. I remember that when the opportunity came a few years ago of making this new departure to which I have referred, the Government said to the gentlemen representing the county council of Middlesex : " We will send an expert up there who is trained in all the different branches of agriculture, and who is able to solve the various problems that confront the farmer in the carrying on of his operations. The Department of Education will pay his salary, the Department of Agriculture will pay all the expenses of sending this man through the county, and if any farmer has any particular problem, such as the analysis of soils, the spraying of his orchard or otherwise, let him apply to this man and he will help him." The Department of Agriculture paid his expenses, and the Department of Education paid his salary, and he was maintained there practically at no expense t<~ the county. To promote the principle of cooperation the Ontario Government suggested that the county council should contribute $500 per annum for equipment, whatever that might be; but I understand that in almost every case this $500 was paid back in premiums given at county fairs to encourage the development of agriculture. Technical or scientific education applied to the agricultural industry has been the means of largely increasing the value and amount of the production of agricultural communities in all parts of the different provinces.

Coming as I do from one of the large industrial centres of Canada, I cannot allow this subject to pass without speaking a few words in support of the views so ably presented by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), and supported by the other gentlemen who have spoken. This question of technical education is not new to us; we have listened to speeches upon it every session for the last ten or twelve years. The hon. member for Pictou is to be congratulated upon having been able to infuse new life into this question. I suppose that the war situation has stirred us up to attention to this matter as nothing else could have done. That being the case, the public mind being alert upon this matter, I think that the Minister of Labor on behalf of the Government might well take advantage of the opportunity to do what he can, in co-operation with other authorities, to put technical education upon a better footing than that upon which it now stands. We shall never do anything in this matter unless we make a start. The old saying is that the man who would play the violin must play the violin.
