The thing for the minister to do is to make a start. I submit that he will never find,the Canadian people in better frame of mind to stand behind him in taking the ' forward step than he will find them to-day.
Technical education is a question of many sides, many degrees, having many phases. But, considering it in its simplest form, technical education is learning how to do things; how to make a great many things better than anybody else can make them, and how to make plenty of them, so that we shall have an abundance for ourselves and be able to sell to other countries. In this way, we would grow to be a great manufacturing country, as they did lin England. We can never manufacture largely if we manufacture and produce only for our own population. There is no reason in the world why eight or ten millions of people should not produce an abundance for themselves and also be a great manufacturing and transporting country.
I believe that technical education will teach us to value things; to know what can be made out of things. I would point out to the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who comes from a lumbering province, that in the forests of New Brunswick the greatest ravages and the greatest plunderings take place. When a tree is cut down in the lumber woods of England, it is used from the roots to the last twig on the top; something is made from every part of the tree. This is done because they know how to use everything: they bind up the smallest twigs, which cannot be used for anything else, and put them up in bundles to be used as kindling wood. In Canada we have an abundance of raw material, but we do not value it; we waste it.	Technical education would teach
us	what can be produced	from
these things; it would enable us, with less labour and with less destructiveness, if I may use the term, to produce results of which we little dream. Perhaps I can impress the mind of the committee, and, perhaps of the minister, better than in any other way, by repeating an expression used by one of the Armours, the Chicago pork packers. Speaking about his own industry, Mr. Armour said: "Nothing in the hog escapes utility with us but the .squeal." Of course, they have not found anything that they could make out of the squeal, but nothing else escaped. That conveys to the minister my idea of the proper utilization of the raw materials which are to be found in this country. If we make the most of

what we have-and we cannot do that unless we know how to do it-our country will be very different from wdiat i't is. I have always deplored the fact that we send *out of this country so much raw material. Why should so much raw material go out of the province of New Brunswick in the shape of lumber ? Why should it ,not be manufactured in that province and afterwards exported to other countries? As it is now, the raw material goes -to the United States; our best, men, boys and girls, follow it and -work in a foreign country moulding out own raw material into the manufactured state. I see no reason why what is being done with raw material in other countries -should not be done with that material in Canada.
A great deal has been said about our copper, nickel, and other minerals. Is it not a pity that we have to send our niokel, out of the country to be manufactured? Is it not a pity that our copper must go out in a -semi-Taw state to be manufactured in another land? Evidently our people have not been educated -to know how to deal properly with this raw material. In my part of the country we are producing steel and iron in large quantities. There is no reason why that steel should not be manufactured in this country -into the finer articles which are made of steel. Why not produce knives, razors, and mechanical tools in this country? Why not make locomotives and engines, when we have the raw material? The reason is that we have not been educated to do it; orders have to be filled in a hurry, and they -are given to firms in other countries. The steel that we produce should be manufactured down to the finest article which is made of steel. If we have not the technical men to assist us in making a start, we can bring them in and educate our own boys; the development will be remarkable. Only a few years ago, the site of the present -magnificent steel plant at Sydney was an empty field. I suppose nobody in the island of Cape Breton kne-w anything at that time about the -making -of iron and -steel; the company had to import new men. To-day in those steel works you will find Canadians, Nova Scotians, mostly Cape Bretoners, doing the technical work in that immense plant. This condition was brought about by the operations of the technical school in Nova Scotia and the night schools to which the hon. member for Pictou referred. I think we have a splendid opportunity at this time of taking steps to 
make the people of this country dependent on themselves and independent of others. We should take such steps as are necessary to develop the vast wealth of raw material whi-ch is in our country, to convert it into the finished article, and to -make the anost of the opportunities that are within our reach. I must repeat that I am much pleased that the hon. member -for Pictou has put this subject so forcefully before the committee, .and I trust that his efforts and the efforts of other gentlemen who -have addressed the committee will hear good results.
Mr. Chairman, in the first place, I wish to express my deep appreciation of the hon. member for St. John's earnest appeal for the restoration of shipbuilding at Courtenay bay.
I said in Canada; I did not limit it to Courtenay hay.

His observations revived my great admiration for the facility with which my hon. friend changes his mind. His pathetic appeal for the restoration of ship-building on Courtenay bay almost brought tears to our eyes.
He did not speak about restoring the industry on Courtenay bay; he was speaking generally.

He did speak about Courtenay bay. He said there was a great ship-building industry there. I have been there, and I think it is within sight of the place where my hon. friend spent his life from boyhood up. During the time that shipbuilding was disappearing from Courtenay bay, my hon. friend was a very influential statesman in the province of New Brunswick, and had great influence in the legislature of that province. During a portion of the time he had a very great influence in the Parliament of Canada. I * have yet to learn that during any of those years he did the first thing towards the restoration of ship-building on Courtenay bay.
I am afraid the minister has not been studying history very much.

I had the honour of sitting in this House with him for three or lour years while he was in power, and I do not remember his having urged upon his party or the Government of which he was a member the necessity of doing anything towards establishing or re-establishing ship-building in Canada.

We shall have to refresh the minister's memory.

Mi1. CROTHERS: If he did make any effort in that direction, it would only show that he had not influence enough with his party to carry them with him, because nothing was done. Although he accomplished nothing during those years, I want to say that I sympathize very keenly with the idea of establishing a ship-building industry in this country.
The minister has been in power now for nearly five years and has done nothing.

I am quite favourable to applying to that industry the principle of protection that we on this side of the House have advocated for many years, and I am pleased to think that, from
10 p.m. his observation, my hon. friend is becoming a convert to that principle. He desires that that industry should be assisted from the treasury of this Government.

By granting a bonus.
Does my hon. friend take that to be a recognition of the protective system?

I should think so; I
think that is one form of protection. I understand that when this Government contributes public funds to any industry, it is protecting that industry to the extent that it applies public funds to it.
I thought that protection meant keeping out competition.

I listened with great
interest to the instructive and eloquent observations made by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) on the question of technical education, and also the similar observations made by the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Burnham), the hon. member for East Middlesex (Mr. Glass), and the hon. member for Cape Breton (itr. McKenzie). But, as hon. members will observe, there is on the Order Paper a notice of motion by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) on the question of technical education. I understand that that motion is to be taken up on Monday next, and I prefer to reserve any observations I desire to make on this matter until that occasion.
It is not arranged to our knowledge. There are a number of motions on the Order Paper that will come before it.

It frequently happens that motions are taken out of their order.
That has been done several times this year.
I was also glad to hear the remarks of the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), and the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) concerning the treatment which we should mete out to our returning soldiers. I am very glad to know that every member of this House, and I believe every person in Canada, appreciates to the full the great sacrifices that our young men are making in fighting our battles on the fields of France and Flanders, They are making the supreme sacrifice there. I sometimes wonder whether the people of Canada fully realize what we are fighting for. It strikes me we are fighting not only for the integrity and, honour of the Empire, for the liberation of Belgium and for the crushing for all time to come of Prussian despotism from the face of the earth, but over and above all things else we are striving for the independence and freedom of Canadians themselves. I firmly believe that a German victory would mean a German Canada, and that we are not, as some people say, simply rushing to the assistance of the Mother Country, as, of course, we did, but that we are fighting for the liberties we enjoy as Canadians, which would be sacrificed if Germany should win. That is the way I regard the war.
I think we all agree with you in that.

I thought my hon.
friend made some observation to the effect that he did not believe there was any danger in that direction.
I am sure we are going to win, that is all.
I am not so sure.
Oh ye of little faith !

From my experience I have come to the conclusion that the man who is always cocksure he is always right is generally wrong, and the man who admits he is sometimes wrong is generally right. No man knows when this war will cease, or how it will cease and while we are in that position it seems to me we- should concentrate all our efforts on the successful prosecution of that war, and not divert our strength in any way whatever. We do a good deal of talking about economy, and about thrift, and about saving, and yet it seems to me that we are spending months here in doing business that could be done in weeks, and spending m&ny thousands

of dollars a day that might better he spent in the prosecution of this war-and we are doing some talking which I do not think contributes to the successful issue of this war.
As for instance?

As for instance? Every word that is uttered, in this House or out of this House that tends to shake the confidence of the people of this country in the capacity and honesty of this Government, to that extent encourages our enemies and discourages our friends in this country, and shouM, so far as possible, in my humble judgment, be avoided. I am speaking as sincerely as possible for me to speak on any occasion or on any subject.
I was glad to hear the hon. member for North Oxford and the hon. member for Edmonton speak about the manner in which the returned soldier .should be treated, especially in the direction of technical education. I am not aware whether it has been stated in this House before-if so, I am going to repeat it now-that the Government have not been unmindful of these things. They have considered them. A good deal of the time has been taken up in this House, months instead of weeks, that they should be devoting to a consideration of the best way of bringing this great war to a successful ending. But, they have thought a good deal about returning soldiers. Many months ago the Military Hospitals Commission was appointed, it is presided over by the Hon. Senator Lougheed, and it is composed of leading men from Vancouver to Halifax. They meet in different places. They have met in Quebec, Toronto and Montreal, and they are meeting in this city to-morrow. Shortly after they were appointed the Prime Ministers of the several provinces were invited to come to Ottawa and attend a conference to consider what should be done for the disabled soldiers. The Military Hospitals Commission, of which 1 have the honour to be a member, was sitting at the same time. The representatives of the various provinces held a separate meeting and then held a joint meeting with the copimission afterwards. Of their own motion, they proposed to undertake to find employment for all disabled soldiers returning to this country as far as it was possible to do so. With the view of carrying that out a commission has been appointed in each one of the provinces; at least, I know there has been one appointed in Ontario. That commission

has established a local committee in'each town in Ontario. When a soldier returns to the town they are supposed to meet him at the station, to look after him until some other provision is made for him and to do everything possible to secure him a position suitable to his ability.
We all perhaps could do something in that direction. If you will pardon a personal reference, I would say that the most important public office in my constituency was vacant a short time ago? I had a great many applications for it as you may readily understand. I looked around among those men eligible for the position. I found a man who, I thought, was eminently qualified to discharge the duties of the office. I knew that his only two children were in the trenches in France and, although he made no application for the position, I wrote and asked him if he would accept it, telling him that I would recommend him if he would. He accepted it and was appointed, greatly to the disappointment of many political friends who desired it. I have succeeded in placing two others who returned disabled from the front, one in my own department in Ottawa and another as a mail clerk on the railway. We all can do something in that direction. If we could locate one, two, three, four, or five, it would amount to something.
Will the minister undertake on behalf of the Government that he will allow members of the Opposition to have the same chance of placing returned soldiers in these positions?
Abolish patronage.
This is a good opportunity for the minister.

I can only speak for
myself, and all I have to say is that I shall be very glad indeed to receive from any member of this House, whether on the Government or the Opposition side, any suggestions with regard to qualified men to fill any vacancies I have control of.

That is a diplomatic
answer.
That is just our position towards both parties.

You might give us a
little more encouragement.

I want to give my
hon. friends a little encouragement. I was in my own town a few days ago, and

called at the house of a gentleman who has been a Liberal for a long time. He had three sons fighting in the trenches in France. Immediately across the street lives another Liberal, 85 years of age. He has only four sons, and all four are at the front. The last one was going to England with a nurse and his mother said to him:
" Archie, when you get over there, if you find you can do anything for the Empire, don't come back; your father and I will get along some way without you." I went to the next corner and came across a Tory who had only two sons at the front. There was another Tory across the street who had *hree sons at the front. When one of these people gets a letter he goes around to the others to read it; they sympathize with each ether, and they are being drawn together in bonds of friendship and affection by this war as they never were before. They are all doing their best, and it is up to us to do our best here. We must not squander our time or money, but we must put our whole effort into the winning of this war, and we must keep at it until the war is over. We realize the great questions that will have arisen when this war is over; but I do not think we should squander or waste our time in speaking of subjects that are not directly connected with the prosecution of the war.
Mr. A. K. MACLEAN; In the British Parliament, and in the Parliament of France,, the greater portion of the time is occupied with matters not directly connected with the war, but rather with the future interests of the country and with conditions which are likely to arise after the war. My hon. friend takes a very peculiar view about this. It is a very peculiar thing for the hon. gentleman to say: I think it would be a great misfortune if the .conduct of the war were left directly to Parliament. It would be a very dangerous thing to leave the conduct of this war to Parliament.
My hon. friend has a perfect right to his opinion in that respect.
But my opinion is. apparently the opinion of the world.
That does not make any difference.
Do you want to be all alone?
I want to have my own opinion.
The minister is up on a lonely pedestal. He is reading us a lecture.
No, I am not reading you a lecture.

Did not the hon. member for East Middlesex (Mt. Glass) read copiously from debates in the British House of Commons, and did not the minister congratulate him upon that magnificent and illuminating speech?

I am not speaking for the British Parliament or the British House of Commons; I am stating my views as to what we should do in the prosecution of this war, and I say we should devote our attention to things that are connected with the war, although not perhaps directly. I do not expect that we should all put rifles on our shoulders and use them, but we should ask ourselves what we can do to contribute to the success of the war. I believe there are many men in this House who do not approve of everything that has occurred in England. There has been a good deal of dissention in the British House of Commons, and I do not think it has contributed to the strength of the English people in this war. I think it has tended to weaken them and to encourage our enemies. But I do not think that should occur either here, or in England, or in France, or anywhere else. I am asserting my own opinion in regard to it.
But, to return to- the matters upon which the hon. member for Edmonton and ttye hon. member for North Oxford were speaking in connection with the education, or re-education, of those who have come back from the war disabled. As I have said, the various provinces have undertaken to place these men, as far as possible, in suitable positions. They undertook, further, to allow us to use any provincial institutions for the re-education of disabled soldiers, so far as that might be considered proper. For instance, if a soldier returned to Ontario blind, we could send him to the blind institute for the province, paying the province a certain sum for his maintenance and education while there. If a'soldier returned insane, we could send him to one of the public lunatic asylums of the province, and pay his keep while there. We could send any number of returned soldiers to the technical

' schools in Ontario, paying the Ontario Government for their keep.
Is that being done now?
I do not know if it is actually being done. It has been considered by the Military Hospitals' Commission.

Do I understand that
soldiers who return to Canada after having been rendered temporarily insane, by reason of their experience in the trenches, are sent to the ordinary public asylums?

I did not say they
were. Eacli case would be considered on its merits.

I think these cases
ought to be given special consideration and treatment.

Of course. I am not going into details, but am simply pointing out what arrangements have been made with the provinces. The provinces undertook to get employment for these men as far as possible, and to use the provincial institutions. We agreed to pay a certain sum for the education and care of disabled soldiers. There will be some soldiers, of course, who will be permanently disabled and never again in a position to do work. Probably homes will be provided for them. That has been discussed by the commission. Then there are Convalescent Homes. There is one in Ottawa, in which thirty-seven soldiers are convalescing to-day. The soldiers who are sent to these homes will probably all be restored to health. We are not unmindful of the soldier. Nothing is too good for the man who has risked his life for the British Empire. This Government and the Provincial Governments, municipalities and commissions, are all co-operating to bring about satisfactory results. In individual cases the results may not be satisfactory. Cases of that kind always occur. One can only tio his very best. This commission, barring myself, is composed of some of the leading men in Canada. They are giving their services.
You are too modest.

They are doing their
very best for returned soldiers, and will continue to do so regardless of any adverse criticism. I think that is all I desire to say on that question.

I am very sorry the minister has made some remarks which certainly demand a reply from me. If I did 
not reply, it would seem as if I was doing an injustice to myself, and treating without due consideration the references of a personal character that the hon. minister has made. Before referring to the question of ship building, I should like to say that I do not wonder at the frantic efforts which not only he but other members and supporters of the Government have been constantly making to induce the people of this country to believe that this Government ought not to be criticized for their conduct while the war is on; that anything that would tend to * create a feeling of want of confidence	in the judgment or
integrity of	the	members of	the
Government would be injurious to the public interests during this terrible conflict. Well, Sir, I wonder if the minister proposes to bring in a Bill of a retroactive character to restore, Messrs. Garland and Foster to their places in this Parliament. They have been compelled to resign their seats in this House because of the investigations before the Public Accounts Committee last year in connection with the purchase of horses, drugs, bandages and things of that kind. If the doctrine of the minister and the Government be true, the Public Accounts Committee were exceedingly remiss in their regard for the welfare of the Empire when they presumed to investigate these matters, because necessarily the disclosures which were made tended to weaken the confidence of the people in the administrative ability of this Government.
(Mr. CROTHERS : Oh, no, the Government took an active part in the investigations.

If it had not been for the action of the Liberal members of the committee in forcing those investigations, Messrs. Garland and Foster would still be occupying seats on the floor of this House. Therefore, upon the theory that the matters that have been disclosed ought not to have been inquired into for fear public confidence in the Government might be weakened,-upon that theory an apology is due to these two gentlemen, and some steps ought to be taken to give them back their seats in this House.
You are misrepresenting what I said.

Another thing. A commission has been appointed by this Government called the Economic Commission, and it has been considering the whole question of what is to be done after the war is over. Of course, it may be that this

Government did not think it would be in the public interests to appoint that commission, but, impelled by the mania they have for appointing commissions, they found it impossible to resist the bend of their minds in that direction. That may be the case; I do not know. But this Government has certainly got the habit of appointing commissions, and perhaps they no longer fight against it. Let us say to my hon. friend the Minister , of Labour that the unfortunate thing is not that the members of this Parliament have criticized the conduct of this Government and the conduct of their appointees, including the Shell Committee; the unfortunate thing is that there is ground for criticism. It is the fact that there is ground for criticism that weakens the confidence of the public in this Administration. That is the lamentable thing. We have the spectacle presented to the people of this country by incontrovertible evidence, that through the appointees of this Government there has been lost to the people of Great Britain and Canada at least $80,000,000 in connection with contracts for shells. The whole of that amount might have been saved if proper business methods had been pursued.	.
Was not the action of the people of this country in forcing an extension of the term of Parliament for another year an expression of their confidence in this Government?

Let me say to my hon. friend that it was distinctly understood- and I for one wish it to be understood most emphatically-that the extension of the term of Parliament was not, and was not intended to be, an expression of confidence in the Government either by this Parliament or by the people of this country. It was a question of two evils: a question of continuing in power a Government in which many members of this House, and, I think, a large majority of the people of this country had no confidence, or forcing the people of Canada into the turmoil of an election while the war was on. Of the two evils, many of us, to our deep regret, felt obliged to choose what we thought was the least, so far as the interests of Canada and the interests of the Empire were concerned. Do not let the minister take any comfort to himself that the extension of Parliament means a continuance of confidence in this Government.
Do not let him think for a moment that it means that we are not to reserve our right
to criticise. When'the right hon. leader of the Opposition supported the resolution for the extension of Parliament he made it distinctly understood that the Opposition reserved the right to criticize wrongdoing whenever it should appear.
You are wandering from my question.
What was my hon. friend's question?

If the fact that the people had expressed, the desire that there should be no election for another year, and that this Government shoWd be allowed to carry on the work of the oohntry for that period was that not an expression of their confidence.

Not at all. It was a
choice between two evils, just as it was amongst hon. members on this side.
You were probably moved to act as you did by the feeling of the people throughout the country.

When the people of this country, as my hon. friend will find* if he reads the newspapers, expressed the opinion that the term of Parliament should be extended on account of this war being in progress, there was announced everywhere in the public press an earnest hope that the Opposition would insist upon the strictest economy in the expenditure of public monies and upon the exercise of the very greatest degree of honesty in the administration of public affairs. My hon, friend, thinks he has a right to lecture us, and, perhaps, he has, but it will not have any effect. No matter what my hon. friend says, we will still endeavour to discharge our duty, as we see it, to the public.
I am only repeating in substance what the right hon. leader of the Opposition said more than a year ago, and what the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) quoted yesterday.

Nothing of the kind. My right hon. friend, in his speech on the Address, said that that was giving a distorted interpretation of his remarks. He said that he never intended to shut his eyes to wrongdoing or to improper expenditure of the public money. What he meant was, that, with respect to the Government's method of raising money for war purposes and of the actual carrying on of the war, even though the Opposition might not approve of the methods pursued, there would be no opposition. establish ship-yards and build war vessels, and their intention was to build them there.

The hon. gentleman has
probably forgotten the facts. Was not there a difference of opinion between the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) and the leader of the Government of that day (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) as to where these vessels were to be built, and was not that the cause of delay?

While the tenders were under consideration, questions arose as to who were the lowest tenderers. The offer of Cammell, Laird & Company was to build at Courtenay bay. There was a tender of the Vickers Maxim Company to build at Mont-

real, another tender to build at Halifax, and others at other places-six or seven tenders in all. But before we went out of office, the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries decided that the tender of Cammell, Laird & Co. was the lowest and returned all the deposits of other tenderers, leaving it with his successor to complete the awarding of contract, and leaving also the deposit of $100,000 of a guarantee. The Minister of Labour says that he never heard of my doing anything.
The hon. gentleman has not told us anything about shipbuilding.
I said that the plans covered the establishment of large shipbuilding yards at St. John.
The hon, gentleman talked about the building of a wharf.
It included also the building of ten war vessels, and there is something else that the hon. gentleman may not know but that the people of St. John do know-[DOT]
There was no contract for the building of war vessels so far as I have heard.
Does the hon. gentleman say there were no tenders?
No, but the Government of that day kept them for six months and did not either accept them or reject them.

I have already said that when we went out of office, my colleague, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, decided that the tender of Cammell, Laird and Company was the lowest, and left that tender in his office, together with a deposit of $100,000 as a guarantee for the carrying out of the contract. When the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) took office, instead of acting upon that tender and awarding the contract for the establishment of a shipyard and the building of these war vessels at the port of St. John, the hon. gentleman, although representing that constituency, returned the deposit of Cammell, Laird and Company and allowed the whole matter to lapse.
Why did not that Government accept the tender?

Had we done so, we should have been charged with having entered into a contract of enormous importance afteT we had, for the time being, lost the confidence of the people. We did not think it would be proper.
Why did not the Government accept them before that?

The tenders were taken home to England by the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Mr. Brodeur, for examination by the Admiralty. The specifications were examined toy the Admiralty and approved. And when the hon. gentleman returned to Canada, almost immediately thereafter there was a dissolution of Parliament, .and there was no opportunity to act upon the tenders before that dissolution f(Ook place. It resolves itself into this: that I as Minister of Public Works called for tenders for the building of the works at Courtenay bay-my colleague the Minister of the Naval Service called for tenders for the building of war vessels, which involved the establishment of a great shipyard and .ship-building plant. When the present 'Government came into office these tenders for the shipyard and shipbuilding plant were abandoned and the deposit was returned. The hon. Minister of Public Works acted upon the tenders which I had invited, and simply let the contract for the Courtenay bay works, involving the dredging, the docks, *and the building of a dry-dock. I am quite prepared at any time to allow my conduct in connection with the development of ship building in Canada to be examined into and to be subject to all possible criticism. I desire to thank my hon. friend, the Minister of Public Works for the efforts that he has made to have the work of developing Courtenay Bay carried on under the plans which I had prepared, and upon which I had invited tenders. I regret that he has not found it possible to proceed more rapidly; I should like to have seen the work of the dry-dock much further advanced than it is. While I am on my feet, let me say one other thing in this connection-the Minister of Labour is responsible for my rising to my feet at all, which is, perhaps, an unhappy circumstance. In my judgment it is deplorable, after the effort that was made to have a transcontinental line built and operated from the Atlantic to the Pacific, that this Government has tried its very best to defeat the whole project. The road is completed between Moncton and Cochrane and

all the way on to Winnipeg. The road is a. magnificent one; the road-bed is the finest upon the American continent. They have a car ferry at Quebec, yet, Sir, they are practically operating only that ,part of the road between Cochrane and Winnipeg. Not long ago-

I was wondering

speechtext: Order.

I was never more earnest about anything in my life when I say that the Government ought immediately to bring down a policy of encouraging the building of ships in Canada. A great many people would thus be given employment; enormous advantage to Canada would result. If the Government do not do that without further delay, they will be guilty of a crime against the people of Canada. That is a strong word to use, but in view of the decline of Canadian shipping, and of the great demand there is for ships, I may say that it is a crime to delay longer the building of ships in Canada and the establishment of a Canadian mercantile marine on a large scale.

Unless we sit very late, it will be impossible for us to dispose of this item concerning the Conciliation Act, because it involves consideration of all
the matters that pertain to the labour troubles throughout the Dominion last year. Speaking on behalf of those who have discussed without party bias the important matter that has been dealt with, I must say that the ungracious manner in which the minister dealt with the question was rather surprising. It appears that the hon. Minister of Labour does not want hon. gentlemen on this side of the House to discuss questions in a non-partisan way. I leave it to the judgment of this committee as to whether any of my remarks in dealing with the question justified the minister in making the reply that he did. He took the ground that by virtue of the fact that this Opposition agreed to extend the life of Parliament for a year, we should sit here like a lot of automatons and register the decrees of gentlemen who happen to be in power for the time being. Hon. gentlemen opposite seem to think that by agreeing to the extension of the term of Parliament we gave them a certificate ot character. That is a ludicrous proposition.
Nobody suggested that.

My hon. friend did not know what he was talking about if he did not try to say that the people of Canada, speaking through us, expressed their confidence in the gentlemen who happen to be members of the Government for the time being. He even flattered himself that we on this side of the House had any confidence in the Government when they agreed to the proposal to extend the term of Parliament. Hon. gentlemen on this side of the House were dealing with these matters in an absolutely fair way, without trying to embarrass the Government or to delay the consideration of public business. We want to get through in reasonable time, but when important matters require consideration, we want to discuss them fairly. If we are to take these items up in order, I think I am in the judgment of hon. gentlemen on this side when I say that we are willing to let certain items pass and then adjourn. But in regard to the Conciliation Act-
